newsitem.title: COMOROS: Hijack plane section, bodies may be raised Monday.
newsitem.headline: Hijack plane section, bodies may be raised Monday.

text.p: Rescuers planned to try to retrieve on Monday a partly-sunk fuselage section with the bodies of many of the 123 people wh died when a hijacked Ethiopian plane crashed into the sea off the Comoro Islands.
Fifty-two people on board flight ET 961 survived, according to Ethiopian Airlines' main office in Addis Ababa, out of a total of 175 passengers and crew.
Twenty-nine survivors arrived in Nairobi by air late on Sunday and were taken to hospital.
The search for survivors was abandoned late on Sunday

Workers said they would make a fresh attempt at low tide on Monday morning to try to winch the fuselage, in which as many as 51 missing bodies are now believed to be trapped, to the beach some 500 metres (yards) from the crash site.
The plane broke into three pieces when it ditched into the sea just off the shoreline of the main island of the Indian Ocean archipelago on Saturday after running out of fuel.
Top African television cameraman Mohamed Amin was among the passengers who died. Amin, 53, of Reuters Television, won acclaim for bringing Ethiopia's disastrous 1984 famine to the eyes of the world.
Some of those who lived managed to swim to the nearby shore while others bobbed in azure waters as sunbathing tourists rushed off the palm-fringed Le Galawa beach to help.
The Ethiopian government late on Sunday declared three days of mourning for the crash victims.
"The Prime Minister's Office ordered that flags should fly at half-mast during the mourning period, starting on Monday, 25th November." Ethiopian radio reported.
Rescuers said on Sunday they needed special equipment to recover bodies trapped underwater in the wreckage.

Captain Bruno Beausse, commanding a team of 15 French rescue divers who flew in from the Indian Ocean island of Reunion, said he would need heavy cutting equipment, underwater lighting and protective gear for his men before work could continue.
Divers had worked for four hours underwater to recover just eight bodies from the wreckage.
Among the crash survivors was the Ethiopian pilot, Leul Abate, 42, who suffered head injuries. He told Reuters from his bed at the El Maarouf hospital that there were three hijackers.
Leul said the three wanted to go to Australia but made no other demands, adding: "The hijackers wanted to make history."

Their motives were unknown but the plan went horribly wrong as the plane, bound from Addis Ababa to Abidjan and due to have stopped in Nairobi, ran out of fuel some 25 km (16 miles) short of the airport at Moroni, capital of the four-island chain.
Two of the hijackers died. One was detained by the authorities on the island. All three are believed to have been of Ethiopian nationality. Their motives were not clear.
One hijacker was reported to have been armed with an axe. Another wielded a fire extinguisher. The third had what he said was a bomb in one hand and a whisky bottle in the other.
Medical sources said three more bodies had washed ashore and divers pulled others from the fuselage on Sunday morning.
The U.S. consul general in Bombay, Franklin Huddle, and his wife also survived.

"I thought I was dead when we hit the water," Huddle said, describing how he and his wife managed to swim free of the wreckage and headed for the nearest windsurfer, which they clung to until they were taken to shore.

"They were not high-tech hijackers -- threatening types in the Middle East style. They let you get up to pee. But they were terrorists and they did not let the pilot communicate with us," Huddle said.
An Israeli passenger thrown into the sea during the crash said he managed to rescue a woman and her baby.

"We simply went into an emergency landing in the sea and I felt a powerful shaking. I was thrown from the seat, and water penetrated the plane, and somehow I managed to get out. I don't know how," Lior Fox, 23, told Israel Radio.

"I saw a woman with a baby who was caught, and I swam towards her and freed them from the wreckage and inflated the life preserver for her, and for the baby I inflated the life preserver, and we got up together on a boat," Fox said.
British passengers Katherine Hayes and Elizabeth Anders told of escaping from the sinking plane with only slight injuries.
Katherine, 30, faxed news to relatives, saying: "I was able to undo my seat belt and swam up to the surface."
Her brother Andrew said: "My sister is a smoker and this may have saved her because she would have been in the back of the plane. I know they were under the water before they managed to get out."
